narrative:
The model predicts you have a 47% chance of failing your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses to help you graduate.

The three factors that most strongly shaped this prediction were your plans after school, your history of past failures, and the amount of time you study each week. Your lack of desire to pursue higher education was the single biggest reason the model leaned toward failure. While every student who passed expressed clear ambitions for university or further study, you indicated you do not. This absence of long-term motivation pulled the prediction strongly toward failing.

Your clean record of zero past class failures worked in your favor and pushed the prediction back toward passing. This is actually better than or equal to the average among students who succeeded, so the model gave you credit for it.

However, your very low weekly study time (under two hours) worked against you. Most students who passed dedicate at least two to five hours per week; your lighter routine added another nudge toward the failing side.

To improve, the clearest step is to rethink why you are in school and what you want after it. Setting even a modest goal for next year can change how you approach your work. Pair that with increasing your study time to at least two hours most days. These two changes address the biggest factors behind the prediction and give you the best chance of passing without needing further remedial classes.
